cells.tense: You're at the bench right now, and your hands know when a piece is done — you set it down because it's complete, not because you gave up.
cells.ask: Leave one finished thing untouched for a week, and watch what the open space feeds.
cells.core:
The work goes well here when the making and the setting-down are one motion — you give a thing your whole attention, finish it clean, and open your hands. Nobody has to tell you when it's done; your hands tell you, and you trust them. That's the practice at its steadiest.

The letting-go is the last move in the work, and you make it without drama. Each piece ends whole, and the next one starts in the room you cleared. What you're free to feed now is the thing already growing on its own in that open space — you don't have to tend it by clutching at it.
cells.sheetLine: You let go when something is done, not when it's failed.
cells.place: the bench where you practice, alone, day after day

cells.tense: Ahead of you, everything looks like it ought to be finished already, and you're pulling your hands off work that's still half-made and calling it letting go.
cells.ask: Finish one thing well past the point where it stops being interesting, and let the doing teach you what release costs.
cells.core:
The work goes well here when you stay at the bench through the dull middle — the part where nothing shines and nothing is new and the shape is still coming. You keep showing up, and the completion teaches your body what a finished thing feels like.

What's happening now is that the ending gets written before the middle is lived. You step back early, name it as surrender, and move on — but you can't release what you never finished, because you don't yet know what you're holding. The staying is the practice. Keep the small light on until the piece is whole, and the release you're reaching for will arrive on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You're calling quitting surrender before the work is done.
cells.place: the bench where you practice, alone, day after day

cells.tense: The finish line is behind you and you're still gripping the rope — the last project, the last role, the hands not quite opening.
cells.ask: Take one thing you've been gripping into your next practice session without trying to fix it, and let the size of the hold show you what's ready to leave.
cells.core:
The work goes well here when you can hold something heavy and keep your hands open at the same time — steady through the long haul, not rigid, not collapsing, the light kept lit because you keep lighting it.

At the bench the grip shows up as over-refinement, forcing the same piece past the point where it's already finished. Holding on isn't strength; it's tiredness dressed up as care. Build back the other side by holding one thing without forcing it — no fixing, no pushing, just carrying it as it is. What returns is the strength to open your hands, and the piece that was ready to go leaves on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You're still clutching what's already finished behind you.
cells.place: the bench where you practice, alone, day after day

cells.tense: The release has already happened — or it hasn't — and you're not saying which, keeping the whole question off your tongue.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, one thing you're done with, and let the saying be the letting-go it's been trying to be.
cells.core:
The work goes well here when you carry what you're growing the way a gardener carries a seedling — careful conditions, no force, no checking every hour to see if it moved. You tend without gripping, and the growing happens while you're doing something else.

At the bench what's missing is the plain word. You practice as if the release already happened when it hasn't, or as if you're still holding when you're not, and the practice runs on a story you haven't checked. Hands know before words do. Tell one person what you've let go of, or what you're still carrying — that naming is the smaller, earlier form of the same letting-go, and it's how the weight comes off.
cells.sheetLine: You already released it — or you didn't — and you're not saying.
cells.place: the bench where you practice, alone, day after day
